sweep_summary: Northern Kurdish (nort2641, catalog fixed-strict final). The sweep produced a single title, Shokri 2002 'Syllable structure and stress in Bahdinani Kurdish' (STUF 55(1): 80-97, Haig & Matras Kurdish special issue): squarely about word stress in this language (Bahdinani = Duhok Kurmanji), but closed on every OA index (Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar) and De Gruyter's site is behind an AWS-WAF challenge; Hasan 2016 p.370 cites it as one of the sources for final stress irrespective of syllable weight, so it is expected to confirm the coding; acquisition priority medium (a peer-reviewed 17-page treatment of the same variety our best held source describes, useful as an independent citable statement, but the catalog is already well-sourced). Held open sources re-read in this sweep: Hasan 2016 (ESJ, open) p.370 and p.379 rule 30 'stress the final syllable of a PW' — the catalog's own deciding quote, whose cite field is empty and whose page locators should be 379/393; Bedir Khan & Lescot 1970 §77-78 (pp.49-50) 'il porte généralement sur la dernière syllabe... dans certains cas... sur l'avant-dernière', any vowel long or short — confirms final default, refines with a small penult class (-ik, concrete -î). No recode indicated; action: fill catalog_cite with Hasan 2016: 379, 393 and add B&L 1970 §§77-81 as corroboration.

new_statements.quote: p.370: 'Kurdish is known to have a simple stress rule that places stress on the word final syllable irrespective of its length or syllable weight (Bedir Khan and Lescot, 1970; Fattah, 1980; Qadir, 1983; Ahmed, 1986; Shokri, 2002).' p.379: 'Based on previous descriptions of Kurdish word stress which suggest that stress is placed on the word final syllable (Fattah, 1980; Qadir, 1983; Ahmed, 1986) ... we will identify the PW as the domain of stress: 30- NK word stress-assignment rule: stress the final syllable of a PW. ... In these examples, stress is assigned to the PW ultimate syllable which might be a simple word as in (a), a sequence of a stem+suffix as in (b & c), a sequence of prefix+stem as in (d), a compound as in (e) and a sequence of proclitic+lexical word as in (f).'
new_statements.citation: Hasan, Aveen Mohammed. 2016. The phonological word and stress shift in Northern Kurmanji Kurdish. European Scientific Journal 12(26): 370-398. doi:10.19044/esj.2016.v12n26p370 (open access)
new_statements.locator: p.370 (Introduction) and p.379 (rule 30 with examples 31a-f); PDF page markers verified: line 535 of the txt lies between the '378' and '379' page footers
new_statements.reading: Fixed final stress, quantity-insensitive, domain = phonological word (stem plus affixes, compounds, proclitic+host); examples 'xoş, xoş'tir, xoşti'rîn, di'gut, guneh'bar, ji 'mal. Exceptions (adverbs/conjunctions with heavy penult, stressed negative/mood prefixes) are handled as stress shift or as separate PWs with phrase stress on the first PW (p.393). This is the very source of the catalog's deciding quotation, whose 'catalog_cite' field is empty: it should read Hasan 2016: 379 (rule 30) and 393 (word- vs phrase-level stress), not 370/392. Corroborated in this sweep by the standard grammar, Bedir Khan & Lescot 1970 §77-78 pp.49-50 (held file lines 2935-2960): 'Dans les mots pris à l'état absolu, il porte généralement sur la dernière syllabe; dans certains cas, cependant, c'est sur l'avant-dernière qu'il tombe. Toute voyelle est susceptible de recevoir l'accent, qu'elle soit longue ou brève.' [In words taken in the absolute state it generally falls on the last syllable; in some cases, however, it falls on the penult. Any vowel can receive the accent, long or short.] — final default with a lexically/morphologically limited penult class (§80-81: 3+-syllable words in -ik and concrete -î), which refines but does not overturn 'fixed-strict' final.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: Thackston 2006 pp.4-5 passage confirmed verbatim in the held txt/PDF; Hasan 2016 domain quotes confirmed verbatim but page locators should read p.379 and p.393 (record says 370, 392). The record's formal quote/cite/loc/grade fields are empty even though sources[0] carries the verified quotation — fill them. (2) Deciding source is a 2006 teaching-oriented reference grammar; it is accurate but thin. Three stronger open sources were fetched sources and all support the coding 'fixed final, quantity-insensitive, word (PW) domain with enclitics unstressed': Bedir Khan & Lescot 1970 §§77-86 (default final stress on all nominal forms, any vowel long or short, intensity only), Hasan 2016 (dedicated analysis: PW-final rule, weight irrelevant for nouns/adjectives), Hasan 2017 (acoustic: NK is a stress-accent language, duration+F0). (3) Refinements worth a 'caution' line rather than a recod

sources.quote: p. 4: "Stress. All nouns and adjectives are lightly stressed on the final syllable. Most grammatical elements added to nouns (-ek, -ê, -a) are enclitic and thus unstressed (miróv > miróvek, gúnd > gúndê, odé > odéya), with the exception of the plural suffixes -ên and -an, which are stressed (kúrd > kurdê´n, kurdán). sources.quote: §77: 'La position de l'accent tonique n'est pas régulière. Dans les mots pris à l'état absolu, il porte généralement sur la dernière syllabe; dans certains cas, cependant, c'est sur l'avant-dernière qu'il tombe. Toute voyelle est susceptible de recevoir l'accent, qu'elle soit longue ou brève.' §78: all non-compound nominal forms (nouns, adjectives, adverbs), most compounds, infinitives and participles take final stress; stress affects intensity only, not vowel quality or length. §80-81: words of 3+ syllables in suffix -ik and concrete-sense -î (incl. 3+-syllable past participles) take penultim

sources.citation: Hasan, Aveen Mohammed. 2017. Northern Kurdish as a stress-accent language. Humanities Journal of University of Zakho 5(3): 868-872. doi:10.26436/2017.5.3.443 (open access)
sources.quote: Instrumental study (30 Duhok speakers, Praat; F0, duration, intensity of segmentally matched stressed vs unstressed syllables, e.g. 'nebe vs nexoşî, 'bibe vs bilind): 'The results indicate that Northern Kurdish is a stress-accent language in that it employs both tonal and non-tonal correlates, especially duration, cues to word-level prominence.' Confirms word-level stress exists and that negative/imperative prefixes ne-/bi- carry stress; silent on default position beyond assuming the final/prefix pattern.

Hasan 2016 (p.370) cites Shokri 2002 as one of the sources for the rule that stress falls on the word-final syllable regardless of length or weight, so the article is expected to confirm the catalog's fixed-final coding; whether it discusses the non-final classes (penult in -ik/-î words per Bedir Khan & Lescot §80-81, heavy-penult adverbs per Hasan 2016) is unknown.
